content: HIV testing services (HTS) should be integrated into comprehensive care and prevention packages for key populations, including adolescents and pregnant women, to improve health outcomes and reduce transmission risks. Below are the key recommendations and practices based on the World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines: 1. HIV Testing Approaches for Key Populations: Risk-based HIV testing can be offered to key populations as part of a comprehensive care package, though the evidence supporting this is of very low quality. HIV self-testing is strongly recommended as an effective and accessible testing approach, supported by moderate-quality evidence. 2. HIV Testing for Adolescents: In all settings, HTS with linkages to prevention, treatment, and care is recommended for adolescents from key populations, even though the evidence quality is very low. In high HIV burden settings, HTS should be offered to all adolescents with appropriate linkages to care and prevention services. In low HIV burden settings, HTS should be accessible to all adolescents, but this is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 3. Adolescents should receive counseling on the potential benefits and risks of disclosing their HIV-positive status. They should be supported in deciding if, when, how, and to whom to disclose their status. 4. Provider-Assisted Referral: Provider-assisted referral should be offered to individuals with HIV as part of a voluntary, comprehensive package of testing and care. This approach is strongly recommended and supported by moderate-quality evidence. 5. Age of Consent Policies: 6. HIV Testing in Pregnancy: Pregnant women should be tested for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) as early as possible, ideally during the first antenatal care visit. This is strongly recommended, with varying levels of evidence quality for each condition. In high HIV burden settings, maternal retesting during the third trimester is advised, especially for women at high ongoing risk of HIV. In low HIV burden settings, retesting all pregnant women is not cost-effective unless focused on high-risk populations. 7. Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission (PMTCT): Early HIV and syphilis testing during pregnancy enables timely prevention, treatment, and care, reducing transmission risks to infants and sexual partners. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is most effective in preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission when initiated before or early in pregnancy. 8. HIV Testing for Infants and Children: All HIV-exposed infants should undergo virological testing (e.g., nucleic acid testing or NAT) at 4–6 weeks of age or as soon as possible thereafter. This is strongly recommended with high-quality evidence. ART should be initiated immediately for infants with a positive virological test result, even while awaiting confirmatory testing. Routine HTS is recommended for infants and children with unknown HIV status who are admitted for inpatient care or attending malnutrition clinics in high HIV burden settings. 9. Partner and Couples Testing: Testing sexual and drug-injecting partners of people with HIV is an effective way to identify undiagnosed cases and link individuals to care. This is particularly important for male partners in high HIV burden settings, who are less likely to test than women. Provider-assisted referral, where a trained provider offers HTS to partners with the consent of the index client, has been shown to increase testing uptake and identify additional HIV infections. 10. Implementation Considerations: Lay providers and community outreach can play a critical role in increasing testing coverage among HIV-exposed children and other vulnerable populations. Dual HIV/syphilis rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) can be used as the first test in antenatal care settings to improve efficiency and cost-effectiveness. 11. Global Health Priorities: The elimination of mother-to-child transmission (EMTCT) of HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B is a global health priority. Early testing and treatment interventions are essential to achieving this goal. 12. Good Practice Statements: Biological children of parents living with HIV should be routinely offered HTS, and if found to be infected or at high risk, they should be linked to treatment or prevention services. National regulatory agencies are encouraged to adopt streamlined processes for the rapid implementation of point-of-care early infant diagnosis (EID) technologies. These recommendations emphasize the importance of timely and accessible HIV testing, prevention, and treatment services for key populations, including pregnant women, adolescents, and children, to improve health outcomes and reduce transmission risks.
